name: liarjs
use_label: Check where a browser contradicts itself
one_liner: Reads what a browser says about itself, compares it with what the network actually saw, and reports every disagreement.

text.why: A browser controls its own JavaScript, but not the network it connects over. liarjs exploits that gap: it reads the fingerprint inside the browser, reads the TLS, HTTP and ASN view from the edge that served the request, and flags every place the two stories disagree.
text.take: Its usefulness is in showing you what a site can read about a visitor. If you have wondered what your browser leaks, opening the page answers it immediately.
build: TypeScript under MIT, split into three parts: a CLI and driver, 19 browser-side fingerprint probes, and 40 consistency rules as pure functions. liarjs.dev runs exactly these checks.

who.role: People checking whether their privacy settings actually hold, and developers working on bot detection or traffic analysis.

start.text: Open liarjs.dev and it scans your browser right away — no install, no signup.

caveat: A diagnostic tool: the result tells you where two views disagree, not who someone is or whether they are safe.

license.scope_text: Use, change and redistribute, commercially too. Keep the notice.

numbers.star_delta_unit: GitHub stars gained in the window, GH Archive events summed to as_of
numbers.method: Star total = the value last checked on GitHub (stars_checked_at) + increases observed via GH Archive since. The 24h · 7d · 30d gains are GH Archive hourly events summed to the reference time (as_of). No score of ours.

images.alt: The liarjs.dev page on a blue background, headlined "Can your browser fool me?" with the browser analysis in progress.

notes: This file was produced by the same build, from the same data, as the tesign.com item page. The text is editorial; the numbers are stored observations.
